Onsen With Tattoos — the Rule Is Real, and It's Quietly Falling Apart

The most common question foreigners ask me, and the answer isn't yes or no.

You have a small tattoo. You want to go to an 温泉おんせん (onsen · hot spring). Every forum tells you something different, ranging from "absolutely forbidden" to "nobody cares anymore."

Both are wrong, and the true version is more useful.

Where the rule came from

There is no law banning tattooed people from hot springs. It's a house rule, and it's not about tattoos as art. It's about 刺青いれずみ (irezumi · tattoo (traditional)) as an organized-crime uniform.

For most of the postwar era, full-body irezumi in Japan meant one thing to a bathhouse owner, and it wasn't self-expression. Banning tattoos was a way to keep yakuza out of a business where everyone is naked, unarmed, and can't leave quickly. Other customers took the sign as a safety guarantee.

That logic is now aimed at a Danish backpacker with a small anchor on her ankle, which is why it feels absurd — because in her case it is. But it wasn't invented to be absurd, and understanding that helps you not treat the front desk clerk as a bigot. They're enforcing a rule that predates them and mostly isn't theirs.

What's actually changing

Inbound tourism did what decades of domestic argument didn't. Millions of visitors, a meaningful share of them tattooed, turned a house rule into a revenue problem. The Japan Tourism Agency has published guidance encouraging facilities to reconsider blanket bans, and a lot of them have.

Today most places fall into one of three categories: openly tattoo-friendly, conditional (cover it, or use a private bath), and still a hard no. International hotel chains — Hilton, Hyatt, and similar — are generally fine.

Whole towns have gone this way. Kinosaki Onsen is about the most tattoo-friendly onsen town in Japan, with most of its public bathhouses allowing tattoos or offering a private option. Beppu has been the most progressive onsen city, with its tourism board actively marketing the fact across a hundred-plus baths.

The old rule is not gone. It's just no longer the default everywhere, which is genuinely new.

Your four actual options

1. Go somewhere that says yes. Directories now exist specifically for tattoo-friendly facilities. This is the least stressful path and I'd take it first. Search the specific facility name plus "tattoo" before you travel — policies change and old blog posts don't.

2. Book a 貸切風呂かしきりぶろ (kashikiri-buro · private rented bath). A bath your group rents alone, usually ¥1,000–3,000 an hour, and almost never subject to tattoo rules. Many ryokan also have rooms with a private open-air bath attached. More expensive, zero anxiety, and honestly nicer for a couple.

3. Cover it. Waterproof patches are sold at Japanese pharmacies and work fine for small tattoos. This only works if it's genuinely small — a sleeve is not getting covered and trying looks worse than not trying.

4. Rural, small, unstaffed. Village baths and mountain 露天風呂ろてんぶろ (rotenburo · outdoor bath) often have nobody at the desk and no sign. Enforcement is mostly other bathers' comfort. This works more often than not — but it's a gamble, and if someone objects, get out gracefully.

The thing worth more than any of this

If you get in, here's the part that actually determines whether you're a welcome guest, and almost nobody asks about it:

  • Wash first. Completely. Sit at the shower station, soap, scrub, rinse everything off. The bath is for soaking in clean water, not for cleaning yourself. Getting this wrong is a far bigger offense than a tattoo.
  • 掛け湯かけゆ (kakeyu · rinsing before entering) — ladle hot water over yourself before stepping in, even after washing.
  • No swimsuits. Everyone is naked. Nobody is looking at you. This is genuinely true and takes about four minutes to believe.
  • The small towel never enters the water. Fold it on your head or set it on the rocks.
  • No long hair in the water. Tie it up.
  • Don't swim, splash, or talk loudly. A 銭湯せんとう (sentō · public bath) is a quiet room.
  • Don't bring your phone in. Ever. Not for one photo.

Do all that and you're a better guest than plenty of locals.

My honest take

I'm not going to defend the rule. Applied to a tourist with a small tattoo it's a leftover, and the country knows it's a leftover — the fact that the tourism agency had to publish guidance about it says everything.

But I'd also push back gently on the framing that Japan owes you the water. A small bathhouse in a town of four thousand people is not a policy institution; it's a business run by a couple in their seventies whose regulars have an opinion. "It's 2026" is not an argument that lands there, and arguing it at the counter has never once gotten anyone into a bath.

Go where you're welcome. There are more of those places every year, and the water is the same water.
